title: No root pyproject.toml or lint config: CI would run without a linter
description:
## What's missing

The repository root has no pyproject.toml, no setup.cfg, no .ruff.toml and no .pre-commit-config.yaml. (The pyproject.toml and .pre-commit-config.yaml that appear under the tree belong to the vendored pyDEXPI submodule, not to this project.) A stale .ruff_cache at the root suggests ruff was run here at some point, but nothing declares it.

Consequences today:
- There is no lint standard to conform to, so 'ruff check' means ruff's defaults rather than the project's rules
- ruff is not in .venv and not on PATH, so an agent or contributor cannot lint without reaching outside the repo (uvx ruff check works)
- pytest configuration is likewise undeclared: 'unittest discover' silently skips 24 pytest-style tests, which is how the OpenRouter failure (hzgb) went unnoticed

## Why it matters

pydexpi-datalog-1-2afe.5 wires both-profile CI. Without a declared linter and a declared test runner, that CI encodes one agent's ad-hoc command line rather than a project standard, and it will be green while blind to lint.

## Current lint state

uvx ruff check with defaults reports 4 findings, all predating 2afe.4 and hzgb:

    pydexpi_datalog/web/review_api.py:1:1   I001  import block un-sorted
    pydexpi_datalog/web/review_api.py:7:1   UP035 import Callable from collections.abc
    tests/web/test_qa_turns.py:8:1          I001  import block un-sorted
    tests/web/test_qa_turns.py:21:5         F401  ScriptedQATurnProvider imported but unused

Whole-tree lint state is unmeasured; the numbers above cover two files only.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root pyproject.toml declares the project, its dev dependencies (ruff, pytest) and its tool config
- [ ] pytest is configured so the documented command collects every test, with no silent skipping
- [ ] Ruff rule selection is an explicit decision, not the default set
- [ ] Baseline lint findings are either fixed or explicitly ignored with a reason
- [ ] A single documented command runs lint and tests
- [ ] README or CONTEXT records that command
close_reason: pyproject.toml declares project, deps, dev deps (pytest/ruff pinned), pytest config and ruff config. pytest is the declared runner with pythonpath and -ra; bare pytest collects all 883 tests, benchmark auto-marked slow so deselection is explicit and reported. Ruff rule selection pinned and narrow (E4,E7,E9,F,B,I,UP), tree at zero. requirements.txt removed; README gains Setup and Validation sections. Full suite 876 passed, 1 pre-existing failure (plz7).

title: Ship the 1 GB Oracle Always Free deployment path
description: Publish the image from CI so a 1 GB host never builds, cap each service so a spike is a restart rather than an OOM kill that takes sshd, and document the swap that makes the headroom safe.
close_reason: Micro and pull overlays ship, plus a GHCR publish workflow. Verified on the real stack behind TLS under the caps: three consecutive reviews, no OOM kills, peak 542 MiB across four services which is 842 of 1024 once Ubuntu and dockerd are counted. Also fixed a production-breaking bug found by this work: the entrypoint derived the OIDC JWKS URL from BETTER_AUTH_URL, so the backend tried to fetch keys from the public address, which inside the container is the TLS proxy's port on a different container -- connection refused, 401 on every authenticated request, and the UI silently fell back to a fabricated review. JWKS now comes from loopback while issuer and audience stay the public URL, because those are claims and this is a network route. Confirmed by rebuilding: real node ids and six artifacts including derived_graph_semantics.dl.

title: Password reset over SMTP, configured or absent
description:
Better Auth implements password reset completely: the endpoint, the token, its expiry, and the reset exchange. It refuses to run for one reason -- emailAndPassword.sendResetPassword is not configured -- and logs 'Reset password isn't enabled'. So this is not missing auth, it is a missing email sender.

Nothing about auth is hand-rolled: no bcrypt, no jwt.sign, no session handling anywhere in this repo. The Python backend only verifies a JWT against the JWKS the Next app publishes. Rate limiting is already active by default (three failed sign-ins then 429, confirmed against the running container).

Use SMTP rather than a vendor API. A self-hoster already has an SMTP relay or can point at one; Resend or SendGrid would put a signup between someone and a working password reset, which is the same barrier the email-and-password default exists to avoid.

Follow the social-provider pattern from bead 1keu: one pure function maps env to a configured sender or none, the auth config and the sign-in page both read it, and a half-configured sender fails loudly naming what is missing rather than rendering a reset link that silently drops mail.

Acceptance criteria:
- [ ] A pure function maps env to SMTP settings or none, unit tested
- [ ] Password reset works end to end against a real SMTP server
- [ ] Forgot your password appears only when a sender is configured
- [ ] With no sender the sign-in page offers no reset link
- [ ] A reset link lands on a page that sets a new password and signs in
- [ ] Half-configured SMTP fails loudly naming the missing variable
- [ ] Credentials never appear in a log line or the page
- [ ] README documents the variables
close_reason:
Password reset works end to end, proven against a real SMTP server rather than a mock: request the reset, read the message out of the mailbox, follow the emailed link through Better Auth's 302 to the reset page, set a new password, then confirm the old password returns 401, the new one returns 200, and reusing the token returns 400. With no SMTP configured the sign-in page offers no link and the endpoint answers RESET_PASSWORD_DISABLED rather than pretending to send. Settings are one pure function with 11 unit tests; partial configuration throws naming the missing variable. 134 frontend tests, typecheck and oxlint clean.

Two corrections to what I told the user earlier. Rate limiting is NOT missing: Better Auth enables it by default and the running container returns 429 after three failed sign-ins, which I confirmed by probing rather than grepping. And nothing about auth is hand-rolled anywhere in this repo -- no bcrypt, no jwt.sign, no session handling; the Python side only verifies a JWT against the published JWKS. Password reset was one absent callback, not absent auth.

title: Adapter-level KIRA tool-call robustness (coerce string commands, salvage parse failures)

description:

title: PRD: Interactive rule authoring — draft rules, first-confirmation trust, personal authored rule packs
description:
## Problem Statement

A process engineer can only browse, load, and run rules that repository maintainers have already bundled. Anything specific to their own organization's standard, or any check that isn't yet bundled, is unreachable except as a one-off logic request that gets generated, confirmed, executed once, and then discarded at the end of the session — it can never be saved, reused across chats, or found again later. The domain glossary already names the missing pieces (`draft rule`, `reviewable rule artifact`, `rule-pack synthesis`) but every one of them was explicitly marked out of scope for OSS v1, so no authoring surface exists.

## Solution

Add an interactive rule-authoring flow, modeled on MikeOSS's "New column" modal (title field + plain-language prompt + an auto-generate/refine action), that lets a user turn a plain sentence into a saved, reusable rule:

1. The user opens a "new rule" modal and writes a title plus a plain-language description of the check they want (e.g. "every relief valve must discharge to a closed system").
2. An optional refine step (reusing the existing `logic-request refinement` concept — the "/improve" idea) sharpens a vague description into a clearer one with stated assumptions and scope, before generation.
3. Generation reuses the existing Datalog-proposal pipeline that already powers one-off logic requests: it produces a `reviewable rule artifact` — generated Datalog paired with an `engineer-readable rule restatement` — with the restatement shown first and the Datalog collapsed behind disclosure, exactly like today's one-off confirmation card and bundled-pack rule display.
4. The user confirms the artifact through the existing generated-Datalog confirmation gate. That confirmation both executes the rule once and grants `first-confirmation rule trust` (ADR 0007) to that exact version — a new trust tier, narrower than and never conflated with maintainer-exclusive `bundled rule-pack trust`.
5. Confirming also promotes the draft into the user's personal `authored rule pack`, a new persisted entity distinct from bundled packs but browsable and attachable the same way (via the rule-pack browse page and attach modal from `pydexpi-datalog-1-2c5`). Authored rules are visibly marked non-authoritative/user-authored wherever they appear.
6. Editing an already-confirmed rule creates a new version; the prior version's trust does not carry over, per ADR 0007 — the new version needs its own confirmation before it runs without the gate again.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to write a new rule as a plain sentence, so that I can check something specific to my process without waiting for it to be bundled.
2. As a process engineer, I want an "/improve"-style refinement step that sharpens my rough sentence into a clearer prompt before generation, so that the generated rule matches what I actually meant.
3. As a process engineer, I want to see the generated rule's plain-language restatement before anything executable runs, so that I can judge it without reading Datalog.
4. As a process engineer, I want the executable Datalog available behind a disclosure, so that I can inspect exactly what will run if I choose to.
5. As a process engineer, I want to confirm my rule once and have it run without re-confirming every time after that, so that repeat use isn't friction, matching how bundled packs already feel to run.
6. As a process engineer, I want my authored rules saved into a personal rule pack I can find and attach in any future chat or project, so that writing a rule once pays off across all my future reviews.
7. As a process engineer, I want my authored rules visibly marked as user-authored/non-authoritative wherever they appear next to bundled packs, so that I never mistake something I wrote for something the product vouches for.
8. As a process engineer, I want editing an already-confirmed rule to require re-confirming the new version, so that I can't silently drift a rule's behavior after I've trusted it once.
9. As a process engineer, I want my authored rule pack to be attachable to a chat the same way a bundled pack is (chip above the composer, multi-pack attach), so that authoring doesn't feel like a second, separate product.
10. As a maintainer, I want authored-rule generation to reuse the existing Datalog-proposal and restatement pipeline, so that validation, safety checks, and disclosure behavior aren't duplicated in a second code path.
11. As a maintainer, I want first-confirmation rule trust implemented as version-scoped, author-scoped state, so that trust never leaks across an edited version or across users.
12. As a maintainer, I want in-thread rule results and rule-pack UI to keep bundled and authored rules visually distinguishable, so that trust provenance is never ambiguous to the user.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Generation pipeline**: reuse the existing Datalog-proposal capability and `logic-request refinement` machinery that already power one-off logic requests. Authoring's new surface area is the save/promote step and the authored rule pack persistence, not a second generation path (per user decision).
- **New persisted entity**: `authored rule pack` — one per user, holding promoted rules, each with its `reviewable rule artifact`, a version identifier, and its `first-confirmation rule trust` state.
- **Trust model** (ADR 0007): confirming a rule's generated Datalog once grants `first-confirmation rule trust` scoped to that exact version and its author. Subsequent runs of that same version skip the confirmation gate. This is a distinct, narrower tier than `bundled rule-pack trust` and must never be presented or persisted as equivalent to it. Editing a rule's logic produces a new version with no carried-over trust.
- **UI**: a "new rule" modal mirroring MikeOSS's "New column" pattern — title field, prompt textarea, an auto-generate/refine action — reusing the existing restatement-first, collapsed-Datalog-disclosure components already built for the bundled rule-pack picker (`pydexpi-datalog-1-2c5`).
- **Surfacing**: authored rule packs appear in the same browse page and attach modal as bundled packs (`pydexpi-datalog-1-2c5`'s rule-pack UX), with a persistent non-authoritative/user-authored visual marker in both the browse list and any in-thread rule results.
- **Scope boundary preserved**: uploaded policy source documents and uploaded pre-made executable rule-pack files remain out of scope regardless of this change — authoring only happens through the interactive sentence-to-rule flow, never by importing an external document or pack file.

## Testing Decisions

- Backend `TestClient` seam: draft → confirm → promote → re-run-without-reconfirmation flow; editing a confirmed rule produces a new version that requires fresh confirmation; authored rules never carry a bundled-trust marker in their persisted or API-surfaced state.
- Frontend `lib` seam (vitest): authored-rule client state and version tracking, in the style of existing rule-pack-run client tests.
- Playwright (scripted zero-LLM provider): full authoring flow end to end (write sentence → refine → generate → confirm → see it saved and attachable); visual-distinction assertion that an authored rule is marked non-authoritative wherever bundled rules are also shown.
- Visual polish itself stays user-judged, not machine-tested, consistent with this repo's existing convention.

## Out of Scope

- Uploaded policy source documents (e.g. a regulation PDF) and rule-pack synthesis derived from them — still explicitly out of scope per the `policy source document` glossary term, unchanged by this PRD.
- Uploaded pre-made executable rule-pack files — authoring only happens through the interactive flow, never by importing an external pack.
- Team-shared or organization-shared authored packs, and any cross-user trust — authored rule packs are single-user in this round.
- Elevating an authored rule to `bundled rule-pack trust` under any circumstance, including repeated confirmed use.

## Further Notes

- This activates existing-but-previously-unimplemented glossary terms (`draft rule`, `reviewable rule artifact`, `logic-request refinement`) rather than inventing new domain concepts from scratch; the main new terms are `authored rule pack` and `first-confirmation rule trust`, plus revisions to `reusable rule`, `confirmed query pair`, and `paid rule-authoring tier` to stop describing this as out of scope.
- Governing ADR: 0007 (first-confirmation trust for authored rules, new this round), alongside 0002 (deterministic boundaries) and the existing confirmation-gate mechanics this reuses.
- Depends on the rule-pack browse page and attach-modal UI from `pydexpi-datalog-1-2c5` (slices covering `/rule-packs` and the in-chat attach modal) to have a surface to appear in; this PRD does not duplicate that UI, it adds a second pack source (authored, not just bundled) to it.
- Design reference: MikeOSS's "New column" modal (title + Format + Prompt + "Auto-Generate Prompt" + Add columns) as the interaction shape for the new-rule authoring modal.
close_reason: Superseded by doctrine decision pydexpi-datalog-1-3ebh.5: reusable personal rule authoring and engineer-facing authored-pack workflows are outside the doctrine horizon.

title: Authored rule re-run without reconfirmation + version-on-edit
description:
## Parent
pydexpi-datalog-1-2yr

## What to build
Running an already-confirmed authored rule again skips the confirmation gate (first-confirmation rule trust, ADR 0007). Editing a confirmed rule's logic creates a new version that requires fresh confirmation before it, too, can run without the gate.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Running a previously-confirmed authored rule a second time executes without prompting the confirmation gate again
- [ ] Editing a confirmed rule's description/logic produces a distinct new version in persisted state
- [ ] Running the new (edited) version prompts the confirmation gate again, even though the prior version was trusted
- [ ] The prior version's trust state is not applied to the new version (no silent carryover), verified at the backend TestClient seam
- [ ] Trust is scoped per-author: verify at the TestClient seam that trust granted to one user's confirmed version is not exposed as trusted for a different user's identical rule text
- [ ] No HITL sign-off needed — this slice is fully functional/boolean with no subjective dimension

pydexpi-datalog-1-2yr.1

title: Add a Souffle-backed derived semantics query harness
description:
## What to build

Add the first deterministic P&ID QA query harness over generated derived graph semantics.

This slice should prove that Souffle can answer one useful known-object topology QA question over generated Datalog artifacts, while keeping the query corpus engine-portable for future deterministic engines such as ErgoAI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `derive-graph-semantics` emits `node/1` and `node_label/2` facts alongside existing graph predicates.
- [ ] A checked-in query corpus exists under `queries/corpus/` with separate YAML entries for:
  - `compare_known_object_reachability` as `supported_deterministic`
  - `classify_pump_discharge_path` as `unsupported_missing_predicates`
  - `manual_valve_before_check_valve_with_exceptions` as `future_candidate`
- [ ] Corpus entries include determinism and LLM-role metadata stating that LLMs may classify/route/explain but cannot answer compliance questions without deterministic query results.
- [ ] A CLI command can query an existing `derived_graph_semantics.dl` with a known `source_id`.
- [ ] The first supported query compares `reachable/2` and `downstream_reference/2` side by side.
- [ ] The command detects missing `souffle` and emits a clear diagnostic.
- [ ] Empty result sets are successful query results.
- [ ] If `node/1` is available and the source ID is absent, the command returns success with a warning diagnostic.
- [ ] The command prints full target IDs plus labels to the terminal.
- [ ] The command persists:
  - combined Souffle program
  - JSON result artifact
  - raw Souffle output files under an internal subdirectory
- [ ] Unsupported corpus entries return structured unsupported diagnostics, not unknown-query errors.

## Notes

This bead intentionally defers LLM integration. Python should orchestrate Datalog generation, Souffle execution, and artifact persistence; deterministic query output remains the source of truth.

title: Ship the first macOS PortLog OSS/BYOK desktop review harness
description:
## Purpose
Build the first launchable PortLog product as a macOS desktop application: a process engineer imports one DEXPI P&ID, connects a user-owned model, asks grounded review questions, sees every PortLog tool/evidence event, runs one deterministic Soufflé-backed check, cancels safely, and reopens the review later.

This epic deliberately separates the generic agent loop from product authority. Pi may coordinate streamed model/tool turns. PortLog remains the source of truth for documents, prepared graph facts, deterministic results, evidence, review history, credentials, permissions, and cancellation.

## Junior-engineer glossary
- **P&ID:** Piping and Instrumentation Diagram, an engineering drawing showing equipment, pipes, valves, instruments, and control relationships.
- **DEXPI:** A standardized XML representation of P&ID data. It is structured engineering data, not an image and not OCR.
- **PortLog:** This open-source/BYOK review harness. It owns durable product state and governs every engineering capability exposed to a model.
- **Pi / pi-agent-core:** A reusable TypeScript agent loop that streams model output, dispatches declared tools, returns tool results to the model, and propagates cancellation. It is runtime plumbing, not the product database or review authority.
- **BYOK:** Bring Your Own Key/model access. The user supplies credentials or authorizes a provider; PortLog does not bundle model usage.
- **Soufflé:** A Datalog engine used for deterministic graph rules. Its result is computed from explicit facts and rules, unlike model prose.
- **Neurosymbolic:** The model chooses questions/tools and explains results; deterministic code and logic compute engineering facts/verdicts. Model judgment must never be presented as a Soufflé verdict.
- **Prepared document:** DEXPI parsed into reusable PortLog artifacts such as graph facts, drawing/topology data, indexes, and diagnostics.
- **Evidence:** Stable references that let a user trace a claim or result back to document entities, graph relationships, rules, or diagnostics.
- **Review trace:** PortLog-owned durable record of user turns, model metadata, tool calls/results, evidence links, deterministic outcomes, cancellation, and errors.
- **Sidecar:** The local Python/Soufflé backend process started and supervised by Electron.
- **Electron main/renderer:** Main owns native lifecycle/process/credential boundaries; renderer displays UI and must not become the authority for durable review state.

## Non-negotiable ownership boundaries
- PortLog owns project/review/document/artifact/evidence state; Pi JSONL/session files never do.
- PortLog owns provider configuration and credentials; Pi receives resolved access only for a turn.
- Models receive only an explicit allowlist of PortLog tools—no shell, filesystem, or arbitrary network tools.
- Soufflé-backed outcomes are visibly distinct from model interpretation.
- V1 is read-only/non-applying: no automatic DEXPI rewrite, silent fix, digital twin, simulation deliverable, OCR-first ingestion, or trusted compliance claim inferred from prose.

## Release scope
- **In scope:** macOS desktop application and packaged Python/Soufflé sidecar.
- **Out of scope:** Windows and Linux packaging/support, browser-hosted deployment, organization accounts, collaboration, project administration, automatic patch application, and multi-document fused verification.

## Dependency strategy
Work the frontier. The Pi isolation proof, local project journey, and direct model connection provide the foundations. The grounded inspection integrates them; deterministic checking builds on inspection; OAuth is added without changing PortLog ownership; the release candidate is last.

## Epic success demo
On a clean supported Mac: install and launch PortLog, import one DEXPI file, inspect its drawing/topology, connect a user-owned model, ask a grounded question, inspect visible tool/evidence events, run one governed deterministic check, cancel a turn, quit, relaunch, and reopen the complete PortLog-owned review without any Pi session file being authoritative.
notes:
## Implementation-readiness decisions locked on 2026-07-29

The first developer model path uses the owner's existing repository-root `.env` variable `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, provider `openrouter`, and model `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5`. This is a local bootstrap only: `.env` stays gitignored and is never packaged or copied into review state. The end-user path is a visible **Log in with Claude** flow using the pinned Pi `anthropicOAuth` browser/localhost implementation while PortLog stores tokens in macOS Keychain and remains credential authority.

The symbolic tracer remains `pump_discharge_check_valve` over the first unbranched centrifugal-pump discharge segment with canonical P-101/P-102/P-103 fixtures. The release candidate targets macOS 14+ on Apple Silicon arm64 only and is a development, ad-hoc-signed, non-notarized build.

## Product position of this milestone
Completing this epic should restore the useful product loop previously demonstrated by the web application—import one DEXPI document, inspect its drawing/graph, converse through governed PortLog tools, view evidence and deterministic findings, cancel safely, and reopen durable review state—in a local macOS shell with a thicker agent runtime and explicit credential ownership.

This milestone is a launch pad, not the endpoint. Follow-on maps may add multi-file fan-out/comparison, multi-file verification semantics, broader process-engineering QA, additional governed checks, and patch proposals. Those capabilities are intentionally not implied by this epic's single-document acceptance criteria, and fused multi-document verification must receive its own evidence and outcome design before implementation.

title: Prove Pi core is a safe PortLog runtime dependency
description:
## Why this ticket exists
PortLog intends to reuse the low-level **Pi agent SDK** instead of rebuilding the generic model/tool execution loop. In this map, “Pi SDK” means the published npm package `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core`, pinned directly and exactly to version `0.80.6`. It does **not** mean adopting the Pi coding-agent application, its `AgentSession`, its built-in coding tools, or its persistence/auth conventions.

Before product code depends on this SDK, prove that the exact published version can be reduced to an in-memory loop controlled by PortLog. The risk is accidental adoption of Pi's coding-agent shell, built-in tools, credential files, or JSONL session model. A passing type check is insufficient; this must execute real turns and cancellation.

### Shared architecture vocabulary
Pi is an open-source TypeScript agent runtime. Its core SDK coordinates the repeated cycle `user prompt -> model stream -> tool request -> validated tool execution -> tool result -> model continuation`. PortLog is the process-engineering review application and remains the authority for documents, evidence, deterministic findings, credentials, permissions, and review history.

A P&ID is a piping and instrumentation engineering diagram. DEXPI is its structured XML exchange form. Soufflé evaluates deterministic Datalog rules over facts derived by PortLog from DEXPI. “Neurosymbolic” here means the model may choose a governed PortLog tool and explain its result, while deterministic PortLog/Soufflé code—not model prose—produces engineering facts and rule outcomes.

## Exact Pi package decision
### Production candidates used by this ticket
The Pi SDK boundary for PortLog consists of **two published runtime packages**, both declared as direct, exact dependencies:

1. `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core@0.80.6`, imported through its public package root. This supplies the in-memory `Agent`, agent loop, governed tool cycle, lifecycle events, and cancellation plumbing.
2. `@earendil-works/pi-ai@0.80.6`, imported through its public package root where PortLog needs Pi's model descriptors, provider-neutral message/content types, model catalog helpers, assistant event stream protocol, or provider stream functions.

`pi-agent-core@0.80.6` itself declares `pi-ai` with the semver range `^0.80.6`; therefore core is not a standalone runtime package. PortLog pins `pi-ai` directly and exactly to `0.80.6` so a fresh install cannot silently select a later compatible-looking `pi-ai` release with changed provider, stream, event, or model behavior. Do not import either package through a nested transitive path and do not use caret or tilde ranges.

This ticket evaluates the compatibility of the **core + pi-ai pair** for PortLog's narrow adapter. It does not evaluate Pi's coding-agent application as the product runtime.

### Pi SDK features PortLog plans to reuse
1. `Agent`, the in-memory coordinator for one model/tool conversation.
2. Injected `streamFn`, allowing PortLog to control how the selected provider/model is called.
3. Injected `getApiKey(provider)`, allowing PortLog-owned credentials to reach the model call.
4. A caller-supplied tool list, containing only PortLog tools and their argument schemas.
5. Tool-argument validation and `beforeToolCall` / `afterToolCall` interception points.
6. Tool-result continuation, so the model can inspect a structured result and finish its answer.
7. Lifecycle events for streamed text, messages, tool starts/results, turns, errors, and completion.
8. `toolExecution: "sequential"`, preventing related review operations from racing.
9. Abort-signal propagation for cancellation of active model and tool work.

### `pi-ai` features PortLog plans to reuse
1. Provider-neutral `Model`, message, text, tool-call, and tool-result types shared with `pi-agent-core`.
2. The assistant event-stream protocol consumed by the core loop, including incremental text/tool-call events and terminal error or aborted messages.
3. Model/provider metadata and catalog helpers needed by later model selection work.
4. Supported provider stream functions where they fit PortLog's OpenRouter or later authenticated-provider adapter.

The motivation is protocol compatibility: reusing the exact `pi-ai` version expected by core avoids reimplementing Pi's model/message/event boundary or maintaining duplicate provider schemas. PortLog still owns provider selection, credentials, retry policy, allowed models, billing disclosures, and durable traces. This ticket does **not** delegate OAuth storage or login UX to `pi-ai`; the interactive login flow is specified separately in `.6`.

### Runtime constraint
- `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core@0.80.6` declares Node.js `>=22.19.0` in its package metadata.
- The spike, desktop development environment, packaged Electron main process, and CI must provide a Node-compatible runtime satisfying `>=22.19.0`.
- Add a startup/build check that fails with a clear version message when the runtime is too old; do not wait for an opaque module or API failure.
- The eventual Electron version must be verified against this requirement using its embedded Node version, not only the developer's shell `node` executable.

### Package present for comparison, not adoption
- `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@0.80.6` exists in the disposable spike because earlier experiments used its SDK and because it provides a useful negative comparison.
- PortLog must not use its `AgentSession` as the application runtime in this ticket.
- Product work should remove this comparison dependency when no later spike requires it.

### Pi features explicitly excluded
- built-in `bash`, file read/write/edit, arbitrary HTTP, or other coding-agent tools;
- Pi `AgentSession`, session switching, branching, compaction, and working-directory conventions;
- Pi JSONL as the durable PortLog review record;
- Pi settings/resource discovery and automatic filesystem persistence;
- Pi-owned auth files or credential resolution;
- Pi UI/TUI and the full `pi-coding-agent` shell;
- default parallel tool execution.

## Motivation for this boundary
The generic streamed tool loop is subtle infrastructure: it must assemble partial model output, validate tool calls, execute tools, append tool results, continue the model, emit observable events, and cancel without hanging. Reusing the small Pi core SDK reduces the risk and time of rebuilding that state machine.

The larger coding-agent layer solves a different problem. Its filesystem tools, coding sessions, JSONL history, compaction, and credential conventions would compete with PortLog's authority over engineering documents, evidence, deterministic traces, and review state. Therefore the intended architecture is:

```text
PortLog UI and durable review state
  -> narrow PortLog Pi adapter
  -> @earendil-works/pi-agent-core Agent
  -> only PortLog-defined governed tools
  -> PortLog Python/Soufflé runtime and evidence
```

Pi supplies execution mechanics; PortLog supplies product meaning, policy, durable truth, and engineering computation.

## What to build
Complete the disposable executable isolation spike against the exact direct `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core@0.80.6` and `@earendil-works/pi-ai@0.80.6` dependency pair. Drive a controlled fake model through a two-request tool cycle: the first response requests one declared PortLog inspection tool; PortLog executes it sequentially; the second response produces final text. Capture normalized lifecycle events and test abort while model or tool work is active.

## Implementation guide
1. Pin both `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core@0.80.6` and `@earendil-works/pi-ai@0.80.6` directly and exactly; never rely on a nested/transitive copy or a semver range.
2. Assert the executing Node-compatible runtime is `>=22.19.0`, including Electron's embedded Node runtime. Import `Agent` from the core package's public root and Pi AI types/functions only from the `pi-ai` public root. Do not import `AgentSession`.
3. Construct `Agent` with a fake model descriptor, PortLog-supplied `streamFn`, PortLog `getApiKey`, one harmless `inspect_prepared_document` tool, and `toolExecution: "sequential"`.
4. Make the fake first model response request `inspect_prepared_document` with known arguments. Make the tool return a small structured evidence result. Make the fake second response cite that result in final text.
5. Record credential resolution, signal identity/state, tool arguments/results, and every lifecycle event in a PortLog-owned normalized trace.
6. Run under isolated temporary HOME/XDG/PI paths and compare the full directory tree before/after.
7. Add model-stream and active-tool abort cases. Bound every async test with a timeout so a lost abort fails instead of hanging CI.
8. Update the fit assessment with exact package/version evidence and an adopt/reject decision.

## Ownership boundaries
- Pi core owns only the ephemeral execution state needed while a turn is running.
- PortLog supplies model selection, credentials, tools, authorization, trace storage, and abort authority.
- PortLog owns the durable project, document, review, evidence, and finding records.
- PortLog's Python/Soufflé sidecar owns deterministic engineering computation.
- Pi must not load auth, add tools, persist sessions, or become durable state.

## Failure cases to handle
Unknown or built-in tool request; malformed arguments; stream error encoded by Pi protocol; tool exception; abort before request, during stream, and during tool; listener cleanup; repeated credential resolution; hung operation; unexpected filesystem write; accidental import/use of `AgentSession`.

## Tests and verification
- Real core controlled-turn test proves two model calls, one tool execution, final response, and complete lifecycle.
- Tool allowlist test rejects names such as `bash`.
- Cancellation tests prove the same abort reaches active model/tool work and settles promptly.
- Filesystem assertion proves no auth/config/session files appear.
- Dependency assertion proves core `0.80.6` and `pi-ai` `0.80.6` are both direct and exact, with one resolved version of each.
- Runtime assertion proves the shell/CI and Electron embedded Node versions satisfy `>=22.19.0`.
- Import/behavior test proves the implementation uses core `Agent`, not coding-agent `AgentSession`.
- Full spike test suite passes with a functioning typecheck configuration.

## Demo
Run one command showing the controlled turn and abort tests pass. Show that the fake model requested `inspect_prepared_document`, the PortLog tool returned structured evidence, the second model response used it, the temporary state directory remained empty, and the normalized PortLog event sequence reconstructs the turn without Pi JSONL.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The ticket and assessment explicitly identify the low-level Pi SDK pair: `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core@0.80.6` plus `@earendil-works/pi-ai@0.80.6`.
- [ ] Both packages are direct exact dependencies, importable from public roots, and the lockfile resolves one `0.80.6` copy of each.
- [ ] Tests/build checks prove Node `>=22.19.0` in the development/CI runtime and Electron's embedded Node runtime.
- [ ] No production-path code constructs `pi-coding-agent` `AgentSession`.
- [ ] Controlled tool round-trip uses only `inspect_prepared_document` and sequential execution.
- [ ] PortLog-provided credential and AbortSignal reach every model request.
- [ ] Abort propagates through active stream and tool paths without hanging.
- [ ] No Pi auth/session/config file is read or written in the isolated environment.
- [ ] PortLog can reconstruct the turn from its own normalized events.
- [ ] Assessment records adopt/reject verdict, reused Pi features, excluded Pi features, and remaining limitations.

## Non-goals
No product UI, real provider call, OAuth, Python/Soufflé launch, Pi coding-agent shell, Pi SDK fork, or durable review implementation.

## Blocked by
None — can start immediately.
close_reason: Completed executable core and Pi AI isolation proof

title: Launch and reopen one local PortLog DEXPI review on macOS
description:
## Why this ticket exists
A useful desktop product must work before a model is connected. This slice proves that Electron can supervise PortLog's real local backend and that a process engineer can import and later reopen one structured P&ID review.

### Shared architecture vocabulary
Pi is only the generic streamed model/tool loop. PortLog owns documents, prepared graph facts, evidence, deterministic results, credentials, permissions, review history, and cancellation. A P&ID is an engineering diagram; DEXPI is its structured XML exchange form; Soufflé computes deterministic Datalog rules over PortLog-derived facts. “Neurosymbolic” here means the model may select and explain governed tools, but deterministic code—not model prose—produces engineering facts and rule outcomes.

## User story
As a process engineer, I launch PortLog on macOS, create/open a local project, import one DEXPI XML file, wait for preparation, inspect the drawing/topology, quit, relaunch, and reopen the same review.

## Implementation guide
1. Define a small PortLog-owned local project manifest containing stable IDs, original-source reference, preparation digest/status, artifact references, review references, and schema version.
2. In Electron main, resolve packaged resource paths; start the Python sidecar with an ephemeral port/auth token; wait for explicit readiness; capture logs; terminate the whole process tree on quit.
3. Keep filesystem/process access behind typed IPC. The renderer calls PortLog APIs and renders state; it does not directly edit authoritative files.
4. Reuse existing DEXPI preparation/render-bundle APIs and digest cache rather than parsing XML in Electron.
5. Persist original vs derived artifacts distinctly and reopen by manifest. Detect missing/corrupt/stale artifacts and offer safe re-preparation from the original source.
6. Display preparation progress and honest failure details. Soufflé is not implied to run during preparation unless a selected check requires it.

## Ownership boundaries
PortLog local files/backend are authoritative. Electron main supervises lifecycle. Renderer is presentation. Pi is absent from this slice.

## Failure cases
Unsupported/non-DEXPI XML; parse failure with diagnostics; duplicate import; missing original; stale cache; corrupt manifest; backend fails readiness; occupied port; sidecar crash; app quit during preparation; relaunch after interrupted preparation; paths containing spaces; permission-denied destination.

## Tests and verification
- Unit tests for manifest validation/migration and packaged resource resolution.
- Integration test starts sidecar, imports fixture, obtains drawing/topology artifacts, stops/restarts, and reopens by stable ID.
- Supervisor tests cover readiness timeout, crash reporting, and process-tree cleanup.
- UI/E2E path proves import, visible progress, drawing/topology display, quit/relaunch/reopen.
- Verify project remains reconstructible without renderer localStorage.

## Demo
On a Mac, launch from a clean app state, import one known DEXPI fixture, select an entity in the drawing/topology, quit, relaunch, and show the same prepared review without reselecting the source file.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Electron starts and safely stops the local Python/Soufflé-capable sidecar.
- [ ] User can create/open a local project and import one DEXPI source.
- [ ] Preparation status, diagnostics, drawing, and topology are visible.
- [ ] Durable PortLog artifacts—not renderer state—survive relaunch.
- [ ] Missing/stale/corrupt states produce actionable recovery, never silent data loss.
- [ ] macOS paths, packaging resource lookup, and process cleanup are tested.

## Non-goals
No model, Pi, OAuth, deterministic verdict UI, multi-user sync, hosted account, Windows/Linux packaging, OCR, image-only P&IDs, multi-DEXPI fused graph, or document editing.

## Blocked by
None — can start immediately.
notes: Reopened after closure audit: implementation is substantial, but native Electron two-launch import→quit→relaunch→visible restored drawing/topology and packaged-resource validation still need direct command evidence before final closure.
close_reason: Completed native Electron import, sidecar lifecycle, durable manifest, relaunch restore, and packaged-resource validation

title: Connect OpenRouter using the user's local environment credential
description:
## Why this ticket exists
Restore a real model-backed review turn using model access the project owner already has. PortLog will call OpenRouter with `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` from the repository-root `.env`, while Pi supplies only the streamed agent/tool loop. This proves that PortLog—not Pi—selects the provider, resolves credentials, and records model metadata.

## User story
As the local developer, I launch PortLog with my existing OpenRouter key in `.env`, see whether OpenRouter is configured, test the fixed model connection, and run the later grounded inspection without re-entering or exposing the key.

## What to build
Implement one fixed model configuration:
- provider: `openrouter`;
- API endpoint: `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`;
- model: `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5`;
- credential input: repository-root `.env` variable `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

Electron main/local runtime loads and resolves the environment credential. The renderer receives only redacted configuration state. The PortLog Pi adapter receives the key ephemerally for each model request. Project files and review traces retain provider/model/auth-method metadata, never the key.

## Implementation guide
1. Add a typed fixed OpenRouter model configuration and an injected environment-credential resolver.
2. Load the root `.env` only in the trusted local desktop boundary. Missing `.env` or variable is a recoverable `not configured` state.
3. Add a minimal non-tool connection check and classify missing/rejected credential, unavailable model, rate limit, transport failure, timeout, and cancellation separately.
4. Inject the resolved key through PortLog's Pi-core credential seam; never initialize Pi auth/session persistence.
5. Redact credentials and provider response bodies from IPC, logs, errors, traces, diagnostics, tests, and artifacts.
6. Test with fake environment values and a controlled OpenRouter-compatible server. Keep the real-key smoke test opt-in and non-CI.

## Ownership boundaries
PortLog owns provider/model selection, environment loading, redaction, request policy, and review metadata. OpenRouter owns model access and billing. Pi receives resolved request access only. Neither renderer nor Python/Soufflé needs the key.

## Failure cases
Missing `.env`; missing/empty key; rejected or revoked key; unavailable model; account lacks model access; rate limit; offline network; timeout; cancellation; accidental secret logging; app launched from a directory where root discovery fails; provider response contains sensitive text.

## Demo
With the owner's existing `.env`, launch PortLog, show `OpenRouter / anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5 / Connected`, run a redacted connection check, and prove project/review files and Pi auth paths contain no key. Then launch without the variable and show a recoverable setup message.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Existing root `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` can drive an opt-in real connection smoke test.
- [ ] The fixed OpenRouter provider/model is injected through the PortLog Pi adapter.
- [ ] Missing configuration and provider failures are specific, redacted, and recoverable.
- [ ] `.env` is not packaged, copied, logged, or persisted in PortLog state.
- [ ] Review metadata records provider/model/auth method but no credential.
- [ ] Automated tests are controlled and make no billable requests.
- [ ] No Pi auth/session files are read or written.

## Non-goals
No API-key entry UI, Keychain storage for OpenRouter, provider/model picker, OAuth, subscription login, cloud secret sync, or claim that a successful connection validates engineering answers. Interactive login is ticket `.6`.

## Blocked by
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.1
notes: User superseded the original locked model choice for this local OpenRouter bootstrap: use provider openrouter with model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash (OpenRouter model id documented in docs/research/rmso.1-provider-configuration-research.md). Do not silently fall back to anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5.
close_reason: Completed local OpenRouter DeepSeek V4 Flash env resolution, redacted status/check UI, ephemeral Pi runtime key seam, and metadata redaction tests

title: Run one evidence-backed agent inspection in a local review
description:
## Why this ticket exists
This is the first complete agent product proof. A process engineer asks about the imported P&ID; the model can inspect only through governed PortLog capabilities; every claim can point to stable source/graph evidence; the durable conversation belongs to PortLog.

### Shared architecture vocabulary
Pi is only the generic streamed model/tool loop. PortLog owns documents, prepared graph facts, evidence, deterministic results, credentials, permissions, review history, and cancellation. A P&ID is an engineering diagram; DEXPI is its structured XML exchange form; Soufflé computes deterministic Datalog rules over PortLog-derived facts. “Neurosymbolic” here means the model may select and explain governed tools, but deterministic code—not model prose—produces engineering facts and rule outcomes.

## User story
Inside an open prepared review, I ask a question such as “What equipment and connections are around P-101?” I see streamed text and visible tool activity, select cited evidence on the drawing/topology, cancel if needed, and reopen the trace later.

## Implementation guide
1. Define the smallest read-only capability schema: inspect document/region, find graph entities, and query bounded relationships. Return stable entity/topology IDs, source scope, citations, diagnostics, and uncertainty—not prose-only answers.
2. Build a PortLog turn adapter around direct Pi core. Supply only the allowlisted capability tools, force sequential execution, normalize lifecycle events, and reject unknown/builtin tool calls.
3. Create a durable PortLog turn record containing user text, answer-posture class, timestamps, model metadata, tool requests/validated arguments/results, evidence IDs, assistant deltas/final text, cancellation/error state, and schema version.
4. Stream normalized events from backend/main to renderer. Show tool calls as first-class timeline items; map selected evidence to the drawing/topology.
5. Use Inspect posture: answer with cited evidence or state evidence is insufficient. Never label Inspect output `satisfied`/`violated`.
6. Wire one cancellation authority from UI through PortLog adapter to Pi model stream and any active PortLog tool/backend work. Persist an explicit cancelled terminal state.
7. Reconstruct the view exclusively from PortLog records after relaunch; Pi JSONL must be unnecessary.

## Ownership boundaries
Model proposes tool calls and language. PortLog authorizes/executes tools, validates scope, stores trace/evidence, controls cancellation, and presents posture. The drawing and derived graph remain PortLog artifacts.

## Failure cases
Hallucinated tool; invalid/out-of-scope entity ID; malformed arguments; stale preparation digest; no evidence; model timeout/rate limit; tool error; partial stream disconnect; cancellation at every phase; app/backend crash mid-turn; duplicate/replayed event; unsupported citation target; reopen incomplete turn.

## Tests and verification
- Adapter contract tests for allowlist, sequential order, event normalization, and no Pi persistence.
- Tool tests ensure stable IDs/evidence and bounded source scope.
- API/integration test executes controlled model→tool→model journey and reconstructs durable trace.
- Cancellation tests assert model/tool stop and one terminal cancelled record.
- E2E test asks a fixture question, expands tool details, clicks evidence, observes drawing/topology selection, relaunches, and sees the same trace.
- Security test proves shell/filesystem/arbitrary-network capabilities are unavailable.

## Demo
Open the imported fixture, ask one known inspection question, watch the tool event, click evidence to highlight a P&ID entity, show the grounded answer, cancel a second turn, relaunch, and reopen both records.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] User can ask a question in one prepared local review.
- [ ] Pi receives only PortLog-owned read-only tools and executes them sequentially.
- [ ] Tool activity and evidence are visible and selectable on drawing/topology.
- [ ] Inspect responds with citations or explicit insufficiency, never a Verify verdict.
- [ ] PortLog trace reconstructs the full turn without Pi JSONL/session state.
- [ ] Cancellation stops active work and persists an honest cancelled state.
- [ ] Errors/partial turns remain inspectable and retryable without duplicate authority.

## Non-goals
No deterministic compliance verdict, patch proposal/application, arbitrary shell/filesystem/network tool, autonomous multi-step project management, hidden memory, multi-document fusion, or trusted answer based solely on model prose.

## Blocked by
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.1
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.2
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.3
notes: Completed the C01 local evidence inspection vertical slice using C01V04-VER.EX01.xml (sha256 a2b172f04e0dcf9a668e158c6dee3b5fd0dd4e9027b572dc39e54470562b809c) and actual pump tag P4711. Product now pins direct @earendil-works/pi-agent-core and pi-ai 0.80.6 exactly, with no pi-coding-agent dependency. A direct in-memory Agent receives only portlog_evidence with sequential execution. Electron runs an isolated Node worker, streams normalized PortLog lifecycle events to the renderer, persists schema-versioned Inspect records in the local project, supports evidence selection, cancellation, relaunch reconstruction, and same-authority retry. Unsupported prose is replaced by explicit insufficiency; Verify verdict labels are prohibited. Validation: targeted 10 tests passed; npm run typecheck passed; npm test passed 169/169 with deterministic test concurrency; active-file oxlint/oxfmt passed; npm run test:desktop-native passed C01 import, controlled model-tool-model, expandable tool details, evidence selection, cancellation, and relaunch.
close_reason: Completed governed local evidence inspection with durable trace, cancellation, evidence selection, and C01 native acceptance

title: Run one governed Soufflé-backed review check through the agent
description:
## Why this ticket exists
Demonstrate the symbolic half of the neurosymbolic product. The model may recognize that a known check is relevant and request it, but PortLog compiles explicit DEXPI-derived facts, runs a constrained rule through the one Soufflé boundary, and owns the outcome/evidence.

### Shared architecture vocabulary
Pi is only the generic streamed model/tool loop. PortLog owns documents, prepared graph facts, evidence, deterministic results, credentials, permissions, review history, and cancellation. A P&ID is an engineering diagram; DEXPI is its structured XML exchange form; Soufflé computes deterministic Datalog rules over PortLog-derived facts. “Neurosymbolic” here means the model may select and explain governed tools, but deterministic code—not model prose—produces engineering facts and rule outcomes.

## User story
I ask a supported verification question. The agent visibly invokes a named deterministic check. I see `satisfied`, `violated`, or `indeterminate`, its rule/evidence trace, and a separately labeled model explanation.

## Implementation guide
1. Select one existing, well-understood rule/check suitable for the fixture. Document its engineering question in plain language, required facts, source scope, assumptions, and what each outcome means.
2. Expose a narrow tool taking check ID and review/entity scope—not arbitrary Datalog supplied by the model.
3. Validate preparation digest/scope, export facts, invoke the established Soufflé engine, parse typed outcome and evidence, and store run metadata sufficient for replay/audit.
4. Use the Verify triad only: satisfied, violated, indeterminate. Missing/ambiguous facts and runtime failure must not become “satisfied.”
5. Render deterministic outcome, evidence/rule details, and model interpretation in visibly separate UI regions.
6. Make the run cancellable and bounded. Cache only when document digest, check/rule version, parameters, and engine inputs match.

## Process-engineering guidance
The deterministic result answers only the selected formal rule over available DEXPI facts. It is not blanket plant safety, regulatory compliance, or design approval. `indeterminate` is a valid result when required facts are absent or ambiguous.

## Failure cases
Unknown check; invalid scope; stale facts; missing mandatory relation/attribute; conflicting facts; Soufflé unavailable/nonzero exit/timeout; malformed output; cancelled run; cached result for wrong digest/rule version; model paraphrases a result incorrectly.

## Tests and verification
- Fixture tests cover all three outcomes with evidence.
- Integration test proves facts→Soufflé→typed result→PortLog trace through the public check boundary.
- Negative tests prove runtime/missing-evidence cases cannot be promoted to satisfied/violated incorrectly.
- Cache-key test covers digest, rule version, and parameters.
- E2E test invokes via agent and verifies visual distinction between deterministic outcome and prose.
- Cancellation/process cleanup test leaves no orphan Soufflé process.

## Demo
Ask the fixture's supported verification question, show the named check request, deterministic status, rule/evidence details, highlight cited entities, and point out the separately labeled model explanation. Repeat with insufficient fixture data to show `indeterminate`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One named check executes through the governed PortLog/Soufflé boundary.
- [ ] Input scope and required facts are explicit and validated.
- [ ] Outcome is exactly satisfied/violated/indeterminate with traceable evidence.
- [ ] Model prose cannot create or mutate the deterministic outcome.
- [ ] UI visibly separates deterministic result, evidence, and interpretation.
- [ ] Failure/cancellation/missing facts are honest and auditable.
- [ ] Cache reuse cannot cross document digest or rule-version boundaries.

## Non-goals
No arbitrary model-authored Datalog, general compliance certification, auto-fix, patch application, simulation/digital twin, broad rule library, or claim that one check verifies the full P&ID.

## Blocked by
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.4
notes:
## Locked implementation decisions — exact deterministic check

### Check identity and engineering meaning
- Check ID: `pump_discharge_check_valve`.
- Plain-language question: `Does this centrifugal pump have a DEXPI CheckValve subclass on the first unbranched downstream segment starting at its discharge nozzle?`
- Scope input: exactly one prepared centrifugal-pump topology entity ID. The model may select the pump ID; it may not provide Datalog or alter rule parameters.
- The evaluated segment starts at the identified discharge nozzle and follows directed process connectivity until the first branch or terminal boundary. It is not the whole downstream plant and does not assess valve sizing, pressure, hydraulic adequacy, safety integrity, or regulatory compliance.

### Required facts and evidence
The PortLog fact export must identify: the scoped object as a centrifugal pump; one unambiguous discharge nozzle; directed connectivity along the first unbranched segment; DEXPI equipment/component class for every object on that segment; the branch/terminal boundary; source topology IDs and source references needed to reconstruct and highlight the path. A `CheckValve` subclass counts; a generic isolation/control valve does not.

### Exact outcome semantics
- `satisfied`: all required scope/path facts are complete and at least one object on the evaluated segment is a DEXPI `CheckValve` subclass.
- `violated`: all required scope/path facts are complete, the segment reaches its first branch/terminal boundary, and no object on that complete segment is a `CheckValve` subclass.
- `indeterminate`: the pump class, discharge nozzle, direction, path completeness, component class, or stopping boundary is missing, conflicting, or ambiguous. Absence of evidence is never a violation unless segment completeness is positively established.
- Engine timeout, nonzero exit, malformed output, stale digest, and cancellation are run states `failed` or `cancelled`, not one of the three engineering outcomes. They must not be rendered as `indeterminate` because the rule did not successfully evaluate.

### Canonical fixture examples
1. SATISFIED: `P-101` is a centrifugal pump; discharge nozzle `P-101-N2`; directed path `P-101-N2 -> PIPE-101 -> CV-101 -> BOUNDARY-101`; `CV-101` has DEXPI class `CheckValve`. Expected outcome: `satisfied`. Evidence includes the complete ordered path and highlights `P-101`, `P-101-N2`, and `CV-101`.
2. VIOLATED: `P-102` is a centrifugal pump; discharge nozzle `P-102-N2`; complete directed path `P-102-N2 -> PIPE-102 -> GV-102 -> BOUNDARY-102`; `GV-102` is a generic gate/isolation valve and no object is a `CheckValve` subclass. Expected outcome: `violated`. Evidence includes the complete path and the asserted terminal boundary.
3. INDETERMINATE: `P-103` is a centrifugal pump but has two candidate discharge nozzles, or the only path terminates because an edge/class fact is missing without a completeness boundary. Expected outcome: `indeterminate` with reason code `ambiguous_discharge_nozzle` or `incomplete_discharge_segment`; never `violated`.

### Required result contract
Return a PortLog-owned record containing check ID/version, document preparation digest, pump scope ID, run status, optional engineering outcome, reason code, ordered evidence entity IDs/source references, Soufflé engine metadata, start/end times, and cache provenance. The model receives a read-only projection and may explain it, but cannot write any field.

### Additional acceptance criteria
- [ ] The three canonical fixtures produce exactly the outcomes and reason codes above.
- [ ] A generic valve cannot satisfy the check.
- [ ] A missing edge/class/completeness fact cannot produce `violated`.
- [ ] Runtime failure and cancellation produce no engineering outcome.
- [ ] The demo question is: `Does pump P-101 have a check valve on its first discharge segment?`
close_reason: Implemented pump_discharge_check_valve through the governed PortLog/Souffle boundary with explicit scope, typed triad outcomes, evidence trace, cache keying, Verify UI separation, fail-closed model handling, and agent/native acceptance coverage.

title: Let the user log in to a supported model provider on macOS
description:
## Why this ticket exists
Turn the developer bootstrap into an end-user-capable desktop application. Ticket `.3` proves model execution with the owner's OpenRouter `.env`; this ticket lets a user launch PortLog with no `.env`, click **Log in with Claude**, authorize in the browser, and use the same grounded review journey. Pi's provider implementation may supply protocol machinery, but PortLog owns the UX, tokens, lifecycle, and review authority.

## User story
As a macOS user, I click **Log in with Claude**, complete the official Claude Pro/Max authorization in my browser, return to PortLog, see honest connected and billing status, run a grounded review, remain connected after relaunch when refresh succeeds, and log out.

## What to build
Use the exact pinned Pi AI package's `anthropicOAuth` implementation for its documented Anthropic Claude Pro/Max browser/localhost flow. Run it only in Electron main. Store credentials in macOS Keychain, pass ephemeral resolved access into the same PortLog Pi-core adapter used by `.3`, and expose a visible Log in/Log out account surface.

## Implementation guide
1. Contract-test the pinned `anthropicOAuth` export and callback behavior before UI work. If it differs from this ticket, stop and amend the issue.
2. Implement PortLog states: logged_out, opening_browser, waiting_for_authorization, logged_in, refresh_failed, cancelled.
3. Open the system browser. Bind callback only to `127.0.0.1`; use the provider flow's state/PKCE protection and close on every terminal path.
4. Store/replace/delete tokens atomically in Keychain service `org.portlog.desktop.anthropic.oauth`, account `default`.
5. Resolve or refresh before a request, then pass ephemeral access to PortLog's model adapter. Never create/read `~/.pi/agent/auth.json`.
6. Add visible billing/eligibility wording and honest provider errors.
7. Run the `.4` evidence-backed inspection through this login route and record only provider/model/auth-method metadata.

## Ownership boundaries
PortLog owns login UX, callback lifecycle, token storage references, refresh policy, logout, model selection, review traces, and cancellation. Keychain stores secrets at rest. Pi provider code supplies the official protocol implementation but is not credential or session authority.

## Failure cases
Browser cancellation; timeout; callback port unavailable; state/PKCE mismatch; replay/duplicate callback; app quit during login; Keychain denial; expired/revoked token; refresh failure; offline provider; account ineligible; extra usage required; token in URL/error/log; logout during an active request.

## Demo
On a Mac with no `.env`: launch PortLog, click **Log in with Claude**, finish browser authorization, run the existing grounded DEXPI inspection, quit/relaunch, verify connected status or refresh, log out, and prove no tokens exist in project files, review artifacts, renderer state, or Pi auth paths.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A visible Log in with Claude / Log out flow works without `.env`.
- [ ] The exact pinned `anthropicOAuth` flow is contract-tested and version-recorded.
- [ ] Callback security, timeout, cancellation, replay rejection, and listener cleanup are tested.
- [ ] Tokens exist only in Keychain and ephemeral Electron-main memory.
- [ ] Login drives the same grounded inspection without changing PortLog evidence/tool ownership.
- [ ] Relaunch, refresh failure, expiry, and logout produce explicit recoverable states.
- [ ] Billing wording does not promise that a Claude subscription includes PortLog usage.
- [ ] No Pi auth/session files are read or written.

## Non-goals
No additional OAuth providers, hosted callback, team identity, credential sync, bundled usage, entitlement guarantee, Windows/Linux integration, or migration of PortLog review state into Pi sessions.

## Blocked by
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.3
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.4
notes: Completed PortLog-owned macOS Claude login. Added exact pinned @earendil-works/pi-ai 0.80.6 OAuth contract tests for PKCE, loopback redirect, state mismatch, callback cleanup/replay, and one-time token exchange. Added macOS Keychain service org.portlog.desktop.anthropic.oauth/account default with redacted errors and ephemeral Electron-main credentials. Added controller lifecycle states, timeout/cancellation/logout/refresh recovery, Electron IPC/preload, Claude account UI and honest billing wording. Routed the same governed PortLog evidence inspection through Anthropic messages or OpenRouter while preserving the PortLog-only tool. Native no-.env acceptance covers OpenRouter missing state, Claude logged_out, Log in with Claude, and billing wording. Validation after formatting: targeted 17/17, full frontend 178/178, typecheck passed, active-file oxlint/oxfmt passed, native Electron acceptance passed, git diff --check passed.

title: Package and verify the first macOS PortLog release candidate
description:
## Why this ticket exists
Turn the proven slices into one installable artifact that works on a clean Mac without developer runtimes or a hosted PortLog account. Packaging must preserve the same authority and security boundaries as development.

### Shared architecture vocabulary
Pi is only the generic streamed model/tool loop. PortLog owns documents, prepared graph facts, evidence, deterministic results, credentials, permissions, review history, and cancellation. A P&ID is an engineering diagram; DEXPI is its structured XML exchange form; Soufflé computes deterministic Datalog rules over PortLog-derived facts. “Neurosymbolic” here means the model may select and explain governed tools, but deterministic code—not model prose—produces engineering facts and rule outcomes.

## Supported scope
macOS only. Choose and document the minimum macOS version and CPU architectures actually shipped (Apple Silicon required; Universal/x64 only if verified). Windows and Linux are explicitly deferred.

## User journey
Install PortLog, launch it, pass first-run checks, import one DEXPI P&ID, inspect drawing/topology, connect via the supported BYOK method, ask a grounded question, inspect evidence, run the deterministic check, cancel a turn, quit, relaunch, and reopen the review.

## Implementation guide
1. Package Electron renderer/main plus a self-contained Python backend and Soufflé executable/resources. The user must not install Python, Node, or Soufflé separately.
2. Resolve all resources relative to packaged app paths, not source-tree working directories. Support paths with spaces and read-only app bundle contents.
3. Define first-run local data/log/cache locations and permissions. Keep credentials in Keychain and projects user-visible/portable.
4. Supervise sidecar readiness, health, crash, restart policy, process-tree termination, and per-launch secret/port handoff. Never expose backend broadly on the network.
5. Configure signing/notarization if distribution requires it; document Gatekeeper behavior, entitlements, architecture, and update policy. Do not imply notarization if not completed.
6. Add an acceptance harness/checklist for a clean supported Mac and collect artifact sizes/startup/preparation/turn/check timings. Performance measurement informs limits; GUI choice is not treated as a compute fix.
7. Produce actionable diagnostics export with secrets redacted.

## Ownership boundaries
Packaged Electron remains launcher/presentation; PortLog sidecar/local artifacts remain review authority; Pi remains in-memory runtime plumbing; Keychain remains secret authority; Soufflé remains deterministic engine.

## Failure cases
Damaged/unsigned/quarantined app; unsupported macOS/architecture; missing execute permission; resource path break; sidecar/Soufflé cannot launch; blocked localhost; crash/orphan process; no disk space; unwritable project; Keychain denial; offline model; corrupt project; interrupted preparation/turn/check; update/reinstall preserves or loses data unexpectedly; diagnostics leak secrets.

## Tests and verification
- Packaged-resource tests run against the built app, not only source mode.
- Clean-machine smoke test with no development toolchain.
- Full journey E2E and relaunch persistence test.
- Process cleanup tests after normal quit, force quit, backend crash, and cancellation.
- Security checks for localhost binding, secret redaction, tool allowlist, and absence of Pi auth/session authority.
- Fixture-based deterministic check and evidence highlighting.
- Record package/artifact size and representative timings; compare to documented budgets where available.

## Demo
Starting from a clean supported Mac user account, install/launch the release candidate and complete the entire epic success journey. Show app version, backend/Soufflé health, redacted diagnostics, project persistence, and no required hosted PortLog account.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Installable macOS artifact contains all required local runtime components.
- [ ] Clean Mac requires no separate Node, Python, or Soufflé installation.
- [ ] Complete import→inspection→evidence→deterministic-check→cancel→reopen journey passes.
- [ ] Sidecar is localhost-scoped, supervised, and leaves no orphan processes.
- [ ] Credentials and diagnostics remain redacted and Keychain-owned.
- [ ] Supported macOS version/architectures, signing/notarization status, data locations, and recovery steps are explicit.
- [ ] Package size and representative workload timings are recorded.
- [ ] Windows and Linux are clearly documented as out of scope, not silently unsupported.

## Non-goals
No Windows/Linux build, browser deployment, hosted account, collaboration, auto-update service unless separately approved, automatic DEXPI modification, OCR, simulation/digital twin, or production-scale concurrency claim.

## Blocked by
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.2
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.5
- pydexpi-datalog-1-34eu.6
notes:
## Locked release target — do not choose a platform matrix in this ticket

### Supported target
- Minimum operating system: macOS 14 Sonoma.
- CPU architecture: Apple Silicon `arm64` only (M1 or newer).
- Package: arm64 DMG containing an arm64 Electron app, self-contained arm64 Python sidecar, and arm64 Soufflé executable/resources.
- Intel/x64, Universal binaries, macOS 13 and earlier, Windows, and Linux are explicitly unsupported in this release candidate.
- Test baseline: a clean standard (non-admin after installation) user account on an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 14.x or newer, no Homebrew, Node, Python, or Soufflé installed.

### Distribution status for this ticket
This is a development release candidate, not a public production release. Produce an ad-hoc-signed local build and document the exact Gatekeeper launch steps. Apple Developer ID signing, notarization, stapling, auto-update, and public download hosting are out of scope unless credentials and a separate distribution ticket are approved. The UI/docs must say `Development release candidate—not notarized`; do not imply normal public-install trust.

### Exact clean-machine demonstration
1. Copy/mount the DMG on a clean Apple Silicon macOS 14+ account and follow the documented Gatekeeper step.
2. Launch without a terminal and show Electron, Python sidecar, and Soufflé health/version diagnostics.
3. Import the canonical DEXPI fixture, prepare it, and display its drawing/topology.
4. Connect Anthropic using one supported BYOK path; ask the P-101 grounded inspection question and select its evidence.
5. Run `pump_discharge_check_valve` for P-101 and show `satisfied` separately from model prose.
6. Start and cancel a turn; show a durable cancelled trace and no surviving child process.
7. Quit, relaunch, and reopen the same review without reimporting.
8. Export redacted diagnostics showing app/runtime versions, arm64 architecture, paths, health, sizes, and timings—but no API keys/tokens or model content.

### Fixed local paths
- Application support/state: `~/Library/Application Support/PortLog/`.
- Cache/rebuildable prepared artifacts: `~/Library/Caches/PortLog/`.
- Logs: `~/Library/Logs/PortLog/`.
- Credentials/tokens: macOS Keychain only.
- User projects: user-selected folders; never hidden inside the app bundle.
The `.app` bundle is read-only at runtime. All bundled resource lookup must use packaged resource paths and pass when the DMG/app path contains spaces.

### Additional acceptance criteria
- [ ] The built artifact reports macOS 14+ and arm64 as its only supported target and fails early with a clear message elsewhere.
- [ ] `file`/equivalent verification confirms all executable components are arm64-compatible.
- [ ] The complete eight-step clean-machine demonstration passes without developer runtimes.
- [ ] Ad-hoc signing and non-notarized status are accurately documented; public distribution is not claimed.
- [ ] Normal quit, forced app termination, sidecar crash, Soufflé cancellation, and failed launch leave no PortLog-owned orphan processes.


## Occupied-port lifecycle evidence — 2026-08-01

The isolated packaged reproduction used a fresh temporary userData directory and a blocker PID on 127.0.0.1:8000. Before the fix, Electron launch resolved but no window was created: startSidecar stalled on an unbounded HTTP fetch to /openapi.json because the blocker accepted TCP without responding. No Python sidecar was spawned and no startup error surfaced; explicit Playwright app.close() then exited Electron.

The minimal fix replaces that HTTP preflight with a 1-second TCP connect probe. A successful connection produces the bounded occupied-port startup error; ECONNREFUSED permits startup. The isolated post-fix run observed blocker PID 54517, Electron PID 54521, startup error at 2190ms, Electron exit code 1 at 2222ms, no window, resolved app.close(), blocker cleanup, and final empty lsof/ps checks for PortLog, Electron, Python, sidecar, and blocker processes. The complete release verification was intentionally not run.

## Clean combined release verification — 2026-08-01

Packaging and release-stage verification were committed separately as 0a1267f and e73f6fb, then tested from clean checkout e73f6fb3f3437edd438dbe7bb8cea31206e89541. npm ci passed. Packaging produced the arm64 DMG/app and the release-stage tests plus packaged smoke passed (startup_ms=4304, app size 714919838 bytes). The complete desktop:verify command then hung in scripts/verify-macos-release.mjs during finally { await instance.close(); } after writing frontend/release/acceptance-results.json; native journey acceptance did not start. The final verification log is /tmp/portlog-release-e73f6fb-sibling-verify.log. The temporary clean worktree was cleaned up; no release-owned process or port 8000/3000 listener remains. Bead stays in progress.
close_reason: Packaged arm64 release now passes the complete native journey; fixed OAuth hydration, persisted desktop provider selection, refreshed packaged OpenRouter resolution, and verified clean startup/cleanup.

title: Split generated EDB from reusable graph topology IDB
description:
## Parent

- pydexpi-datalog-1-153 PRD: Build a deterministic P&ID QA query layer

## What to build

Split the generated Datalog EDB from reusable Datalog IDB rules so Datalog becomes the source of truth for classification policy and graph topology semantics, while Python remains the Adapter that emits EDB from graph_facts.json and assembles executable artifacts.

Use lowercase Datalog directories:
